abasto-patio-comidas: We looked into the original morphologies of fairs and markets.
The origin of the polis and the market's first home. A meeting point, a place that calls people together.
A natural event. A space of interaction. A centre of eco-perceived sustainability.

The proposal starts from the idea of rebuilding the DNA of sustainable public space inside the shopping centre, recreating green areas for leisure. Far from bringing in real nature, we emulate an organic universe that is deliberately orthogonal, built as a topographic chequerboard.
We recreate a picnic setting through the eco-perception of several of its elements as a design strategy. Its sustainable materials are part of the same message.
We claim the spontaneous and deliberate gathering of mixed uses, typical of a contemporary city, as the only viable proposal for today's commercial spaces. We divided these into cells and named them:
Eco-wellbeing: green areas recreated for gastronomic use (picnic).
Play: leisure spaces built through topographic configurations.
Connectivity: areas set up ergonomically, with specific furniture, for remote work (networking).
Market: areas beneath the atria (stands) for commercial units that ideally complement the new use of the leisure areas.

These four cells make up a set of mixed uses and stand for a dynamism ready to host every kind of visitor. Two large atria, I and II, work as viewpoints from which to see and be seen, coexisting with and resolving both leisure and gastronomic uses. There is a great deal of history behind the Abasto shopping centre, and we considered it essential to build an independent identity so that this space has a life of its own.
accor-hotels: It is impossible to ignore that hotels today base their proposals on themed aesthetics and social activities designed for their guests' enjoyment, and this is an undeniable advantage over short-term accommodation such as Airbnb. So why is Airbnb a threat to the hotel business? Or why do most hotels base their proposals on themed or story-driven concepts? Today, Airbnb is like living at home. Hotels, by contrast, are places of transit: despite their renewed thematic proposals, they dress and undress according to fashion, without a clear identity. This reveals a lack of identity.

Our proposal can be summed up in two words: identity and community, both addressed as part of the hotel's operation and entertainment. Identity is an integration of concepts that define an individual or an object, but the hotel should not have a fixed identity; rather, it should serve as a container. A large framework that each guest can fill with their belongings, just as they would at home. A truly tailored offer.

The composition must follow a coherent system that gives it unity. We do not conceive interior architecture as a collection of individual elements: decorative objects, furniture and lighting. Our proposal is defined by a broad group of pieces that form a space in themselves. This allows multiple possible configurations for use in new hotels or in existing hotels undergoing renovation.

Together, these pieces form a living organism that is versatile and adaptable to each key space in the hotel, shaping and organising everything from lighting to fixed and movable equipment. In addition to its organisational role, the system also has a symbolic one: through its old suitcases, it holds the personal objects of every traveller who passes through the hotel. The stamps on those old suitcases - evidence of journeys through different states and provinces - become part of the local identity expressed in a wallpaper. Through visual communication, we emphasise the citizens' shared local identity with a large video wall at the front desk. We also propose the active presence of the most representative local flora. All of these elements are brought together in a single connecting construction system.

It is a void, defined as such by a pure and simple aesthetic. It is free of imposed styling, although its lines undoubtedly construct a universe associated with the modern rejection of eclecticism and ornament, and with the status of the contemporary individual. Today, that restraint is called minimalism: life with only what is essential and necessary. Something truly timeless. The minimum invites us to reflect on a way of life based on limited, measured, basic and sustainable consumption.

The contemporary traveller knows that a carry-on can hold everything they need. We believe that today a camera, a laptop for writing, a book for reading or a notebook for drawing is undoubtedly more valuable than two suitcases full of clothes. These are the objects that define part of our identity. The value of the emotional over the material. Identity is universal: it is the aspect that defines us.
aire-libre: Every decision in this project was conceived under the same approach: we sought to create a botanical oasis located in the middle of urban chaos. This guiding line marked a north that determined each of the project definitions from the architectural space, through the choice of materials, equipment, graphic resources, and mainly landscape interventions.

Inspired by the old ‘green houses’ of late 19th century England, these large prefabricated steel and glass constructions that in the midst of the industrial revolution housed both the exuberance of the wild vegetation of the new continents and the gatherings of royalty, in AIRE LIBRE we seek to reflect this same duality in contemporary architectural language: the rusticity of a greenhouse together with the sophistication of the high cocktail bar. The old glass panes are now modulated translucent polycarbonate plates that form both interior and exterior facades, and the old steel structures are replaced by metal frames that modulate these facades.

In the same sense, the gastronomic proposal is also eclectic in its approach, classic but modern, made possible by combining a wood-fired kitchen with a large handmade clay oven, accompanied by a high-tech and technically complex kitchen, both of which are complementary and visible.

The project is developed over two floors, totalling more than 900m2 between indoors and outdoors. From an access foyer that acts as a reception, the spaces are articulated integrating open and closed, covered and uncovered areas, all of them always approached under the same conceptual treatment, from the material, lighting and biophilia strategies, generating as a result the indefinition between inside and outside.

The chromatic and material palette was always governed by the decision of nature and the nobility of its materials, both in interiors and exteriors. Textures of polished and hammered concrete, solid wood openings, added to stone cladding, granite crusts on the bar fronts, aged mirrors and the use of reclaimed wood planks, accompanied by the abundance of botanical plants in every corner of the premises, perfectly achieve the desired ambience.

This project could not be sustained without having resolved, in the first place, the high degree of maintenance required by the vegetation. A complex automated irrigation network was designed by a closed circuit of circulating fertilised water that works in conjunction with lighting equipment that is activated in counter-time with the use of the premises, to guarantee irrigation and photosynthesis in all the plants, both indoors and outdoors. To complete this system, a network of foggers was installed in all the outdoor spaces which, on particularly hot days, spray water droplets into the air, guaranteeing coolness and comfort for users.
The serenity of the spaces and materials, in contrast to the technical complexity of the project, resulted in spaces for meeting and enjoyment in the outdoor.
antiche: Antiche Tentazioni is an ice cream shop with an Italian character, from its equipment and owners to the type of product it offers. This led us to use aesthetic devices that recall the Italian region of Tuscany. Its appearance is defined by elements in predominantly terracotta tones, the choice of cement tiles, the presence of traditional tiled roofs and, unmistakably, the weathered condition created by the passage of time.

Far from attempting to reproduce the old, we reconfigured it through a contemporary abstraction. To do so, we incorporated the arch, the ancient construction element par excellence and a defining feature of Italian architecture throughout history.

One of the elements we defined as part of its DNA is the broken cement tile, a symbol of the passage of time. Another is the colonial roof tile, reinterpreted in its use as a lighting support. The fixtures were specially designed around curves, roof tiles and vegetation.
The arches are finished in an aged-gold effect, while the surfaces they outline are covered with metal mesh featuring an arabesque pattern.

At night, the image of the project reinforces the arches as its essential feature. The metal mesh that becomes prominent along the counter once again recalls ancient Roman arches. All these elements with historical echoes have been playfully reinterpreted through a contemporary language.
araoz: Given its location in Villa Crespo, just blocks from Palermo and in a neighbourhood in constant transformation — gastronomic, cultural, artistic — the A757 project sets out to answer the demand for studio and one-bedroom flats with units of real spatial quality, whether for residential, tourist or professional use.

The building sits mid-block on a 438 m² plot, with a total built area of 2,012 m². It rises from an open ground floor plus nine levels, with four units per level forming a single compact, homogeneous, vertical block. Alongside the units there are generous multi-purpose spaces and terraces, plus a basement with private storage and a ground floor with parking. On both the street and rear elevations, the building aims to convey its contemporary character and so hint at the kind of spaces and materials it holds inside. The single material, together with the single colour, brings a blanket of serenity and visual calm to a setting as eclectic and heterogeneous as the neighbourhood around it.

In design terms, beyond making the most of what the building code allows, the layout of the units achieves the flexibility needed for future use as home, studio or office. The choice of materials and finishes, the flexible use of the spaces and the emphasis on giving every unit generous outdoor space guarantee interior quality and natural light throughout.
atelier-vilela: The project took place in an old corner property. It is a typical house built in the mid-twentieth century considered as self-construction housing. The property is divided into three separate units. The actual project was performed on corner unit, which functioned as an old bicycle store in the neighborhood. The main objective was to operate on the existing place through an element that is not associated to what already exists. While there is not a tectonic association (material), there is from the point of view of the volumes, ie, there was a clear intention of representing a game between the upper volume in contrast to the new intervention. Qualities of the new intervention as a sloped roof expresses a contemporary nod to its neighbor mono-pitched roof. For a contrast between the contemporary and the old volume, lightweight construction system was used and corrugated iron cladding were chosen to create a purely cubic volume, thereby releasing the excess of meters to a small triangular patio. In order to give cohesion to the whole, expanded metal mesh was used to sew both the new intervention and the existing house.

The first level is constructed with pre-stressed beams and the second level with a tubular structure about 100x50 reproducing a modulation which is displayed on the facade as well. The openings and protection systems strictly respond to modulation of the new intervention, totally opposed to the old house, whose openings have no projective logic. The intervention of only 66 m2 covered was not constrained to the corner unit, it also had to solve an expansion on an old zinc roof over the adjoining unit. In this way and through an lightweight tubular structure that supports a wide wooden deck we achieved an exterior expansion of the project which is accessed from the second level. As if trying to recall the ancient craft practiced there, the destiny of the new intervention is a practical space for arts and crafts. The idea is to develop activities such as classes of jewelry, carpentry, etc. mostly on ground floor and first level, while in the upper level will take place, physical activities, yoga and meditation.
banco-supervielle: 130 years of solidity translated into architecture. Supervielle’s new offices balance tradition and digital transformation in a cohesive visual language.

Noble wood in vertical slats covers interior partitions and claddings, conveying permanence and warmth. It is not decorative: it structures the space, organises flows and creates visual privacy without closing it off.
Sinuous curves in the ceiling express modernity, movement and digital transformation. They integrate warm linear lighting that orchestrates the user experience without visual fatigue.

An identity palette of terracotta, caramel leather and warm browns humanises every area. Leather sofas, terracotta chairs, digital screens integrated into wooden walls. Technology never dominates; it is always contextualised.

Differentiated spaces: focused meeting rooms, circular lounges, circulations as experience. Natural and artificial light at 3000K create warmth. Plants humanise. Every area breathes the same architectural language: elegant restraint.
The result is neither a luxury showroom nor an austere traditional bank. It is a quiet demonstration that solidity and modernity, long time and fast change, coexist naturally. Architecture of trust.
benedetta: The project is inspired by the dreamlike universe of textures and materials from the Mediterranean world. The most characteristic element is the waves of the sea, which we implemented through two constructive elements on the ground and first floor. Both give a specific function, one of them as a bar back on the first floor, and the other as a long zigzagging bench that organizes the central area of the upper floor.

White tones are the most predominant throughout the space, suggested by the constructions so characteristic of those latitudes. The use of mosaic in blue and turquoise tones is clearly a constructive resource that represents an era and an art typical of the Mediterranean.
The use of white painted wood strips as cladding in most of the space generates a rhythmic texture which suggests a relationship with the strategy used in the areas developed with the waves.
The terrazzo flooring in natural and ochre tones throughout the facility gives the space a sensibility of subtle and tiny stones that integrate with the "Mediterranean mood".
Finally, the vegetation that emerges from the long bench predominates in its tones as if it were the integration of real nature merged with the allegorical metaphor of the sea.

From an organizational point of view, both the first floor and the upper floor are divided into two areas, the production and the service area. They are both separated by glass partitions as a typical allegory of the old factory windows. The restaurant has large areas for private use, such as the kitchens, production room, camera room and offices, representing 40% of the total area of both levels, which guarantees a functional production for the restaurant's needs.
bienal-venecia: In our proposal for the Argentine Pavilion at the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale, we present a circuit identifying six types of intelligence that have shaped human action throughout our evolution:
individual, collective, natural, artificial, emotional, and rational.

While each intelligence operates individually, they interact with one another in diverse ways. This interaction between any two forms of intelligence generates a tension—a state of chaos—manifested through the seemingly illogical expressiveness of the structures supporting them.

From these points of conflict emerges a synapse—an interconnection or relationship between parts—creating a structure that, amidst the chaos, seeks to interlink (in the very sense of *intelligence*) the intelligences in question, while serving as the physical support for the exhibition content. Thus, the visitor traverses the pavilion by weaving together these six types of intelligence, creating five intersections; ultimately, it is these five focal points that display, support, and illuminate the work as a whole.

These five walkable support structures—realized through scaffolding and articulated joints—are arranged within the space in a seemingly random pattern. They contrast with a central, serene, linear path that invites visitors to pause, sit beneath the "cloud" of these various intelligences, and rediscover the capacity for contemplation.

The content is organized across the five intersections according to a chronological curatorial approach. The exhibition strategy for each intersection presents a selection of works that share an integral, direct relationship with the subject matter, following a timeline that begins with individual intelligence and culminates in artificial intelligence.
Personal creativity is organized logically to yield unique solutions.
Logic and empathy balance human decisions.
