The pavilion rises from a combination and arrangement of tubular components and joints forming scaffolding structures—representing humanity's capacity for intelligent evolution—where solid wooden planks provide the framework for displaying audiovisual content. Simultaneously, the scaffolding supports and elevates six suspended volumes that appear to levitate within the space, creating the project's circulation path. These lightweight volumes crowning the structures are fashioned from ethereal white fabric, created by repurposing discarded plastic-woven bulk bags (often known as "big bags"). This reinforced material is typically used to transport sand during the hydraulic fracturing (fracking) process for oil and natural gas extraction in unconventional fields—specifically, the Vaca Muerta formation. It is a material designed for single use followed by incineration. Reusing it in this project aims to highlight the need for ecological awareness, foster circular micro-economies driven by entrepreneurs who reclaim waste materials for secondary uses (*1), and promote a vision of a future defined by energy self-sufficiency and its positive implications for Argentina.

Following a similar rationale and objective, the project's central walkway is formed from a roll of vinyl rubber produced by recycling discarded plastics (*2). Cast aluminum benches will be placed along this linear path, showcasing the work of young Argentine designers (*3).
bolivar: The building sits in San Telmo, a traditional Buenos Aires neighbourhood whose heights are set by the building code. That made a compact scheme necessary, and it led to the decision to place the entrance below pavement level. The building holds 16 units, parking for six cars and a commercial premises.

The commercial premises is on the ground floor, and the levels above hold studio, one-bedroom and two-bedroom flats. The scheme uses a structure of long beams that gives the floor plates a certain flexibility, allowing different flat sizes to sit on the same level.

On the roof there are four private terraces, reachable in future by spiral stairs. What defines the project is the use of two facade planes: a denser, monolithic line, and behind it a lighter, translucent one. For these we chose a palette of concrete and iron that sets the project's aesthetic. Our work generally seeks two-tone materials that do not compete with formal expression or function. The plasticity of concrete let us mould the walls with rhythmic, repeating grooves, breaking the homogeneity typical of the material. The galvanised metal mesh offers a balance between the density of the concrete and the transparency of the mesh itself.
burger-7167: The commercial space is located in Buenos Aires. It´s small surface (735 ft
) was decisive to its compositional strategy, since in such a small space the impact had to be immediate. Therefore, the colors had to achieve an immediate immersion effect.

Having in mind that the product are burgers, the design strategy is based on the single intervention (folds) of the single material (sheet metal), enriching the sobriety through changes of rhythm, application of textured patinas and lighting design, all of which refers to the hot iron of the baking plates.
Its rythm shifts, textured patinas, lighting design, red neon tones, and the scarce graphic intervention are all associated with the leading idea of hot cast iron plates.
cafe-artois: The project is located in an exclusive area of the city of Buenos Aires, within the area of the most important polo field in South America.
The project is the result of a two-factor investigation in related to the company that called us to the Stella Artois project, which we will describe as follows.

On the one hand, the building volume made us interested in refering it to the medieval constructive silhouettes that define the typical skyline of Bruges, which is very typical of Belgium, the country where the brand was born.
On the other hand, the interior work had to refer to the concept of the old typical European coffees of the beginning of the 20th century, very related to the Parisians style.

The challenge was to compose a volume inspired by these old buildings and their characteristic Belgian ceilings, but executing the figure under a contemporary vision, that is, modifying the slopes of the ceiling generating a dynamism and avoiding a regular volume generating a dynamism and avoiding a regular volume. It looks like the image of the typical buildings in front of the Dijver canal or the Bruges market.

The configuration of these ceilings forced us to understand that the windows had to dialogue in a contemporary way with that dynamism. On the other hand, in front of the building is located the polo field, and in the background the skyline of the city of Buenos Aires. The impact of these visuals was decisive in defining the dimension of the openings.
Constructively, we set up ornamented circular columns under the sloped ceilings, managing to mix an eclectic composition.
The interior organization is a typical two-level restaurant and all the visuals are directed to the polo field, hiding the services to the opposite sector.

The complex dialogue between an interior mostly represented under an image of a café of the early twentieth century, and the exterior of contemporary configuration, resulted in a complex eclectic balance of languages. This made it possible for our client to accept a contemporary image in spite of its clear inclination towards an old aesthetic.
casa-olmo: The project is located in the southernmost city in the world, Ushuaia in Patagonia Argentina, where his hostile nature, icy and wild waters enclose the great tales of Darwin. Its port is the place that shelters the traveler and this magical universe has inspired us in our work. The client's demand was to intervene a house of the early twentieth century respecting each of its areas, intervening only with ambiance. The house is typical of the area, belonging to the Olmo family, the first villagers of this city. Cape Horn just 43 km away from the city, was the trigger that lead us to recreate the idea of a magical underwater world, similar to the illustrations of Jules Verne, where the machines of another century and landscapes are the protagonists. We created aquatic creatures, seaweed, scapers and we fuse it with port elements such as compasses, eyes of ox, through pipes, where both the graphic and these elements make up the imaginary of space.

We construct the illumination through nautical pulley wheel with cords, and we used old cartographic images adapted for different spaces, painted in a mural and wallpapered in the bathrooms. The intervention in the bar is made with old beer barrels, inspired again in the beer brand sponsored by the bar, Cape Horn, manufactured in these latitudes. The furnishing equipment with industrial aesthetics accompanies the idea of bar, whose language fuses a very closely related universe with its location, southern, wild and magical.
cceba: The proposal stems from an assessment of a façade that fails to engage with the upper floor, featuring an overly horizontal canopy, signage with little visual impact, and an entrance that lacks appeal from the public realm. Consequently, the project seeks to strengthen the Cultural Center's identity through a comprehensive intervention on its street-facing elevation.

The strategy involves emphasizing the façade's verticality, visually integrating the upper floor, creating transitional elements to mediate the relationship between the interior and the street, and establishing a clear, recognizable institutional presence. To achieve this, the design proposes a new laser-cut, perforated metal skin — finished with an off-white powder coating — that reinterprets historical references such as Catalan vaults, colonial roof tiles, and wrought iron through a contemporary architectural language.

The integration of RGB LED lighting and interactive screens transforms the façade into a dynamic medium for communication and cultural activities, turning the building into a new urban landmark with a flexible, contemporary image that reflects the institution's character.
cerveceria-austral: Aiming to bring the essence of the far south to the heart of the Chilean capital, Joseph Fischer's design is conceived as a brand experience; rather than telling stories literally, the narrative unfolds through atmospheres, sensations, and materials inspired by Patagonia, creating a space that is instantly recognizable, authentic, and memorable for customers.

The concept envisions an urban sanctuary — a place where customers can disconnect and immerse themselves in an experience rooted in the brand's origins: the power of the landscape, the extreme climate, and the tradition of beer brewing.

Patagonian culture is also central to the concept. Local traditions, crafts, and attire inspire the spatial layout and interior design, reinterpreted through a contemporary lens using layers, textures, and patterns that establish identity without relying on obvious decorative elements. This approach crafts a subtle yet powerful narrative, aligning with a robust, sophisticated brand image designed to endure — much like the local traditions themselves.
cien: The project stands as an ephemeral and fleeting space, destined to itinerate after its mere 100 nights of public use, as its name suggests. This denomination constituted the foundational seed of the concept. The use of dry construction materials has been decisive in its aesthetic and its function as an ephemeral structure. Unpainted gypsum rock panels, Construction Safety Netting, Flexible Air Conditioner Ducting Vent Tubing, Translucent Polycarbonate Sheets, Gypsum Board Metal Profiles, aluminum-foil-faced-blanket, and Steel Reinforcing Mesh—all these elements exposed and hierarchically organized.

Its construction rises with the lightness characteristic of a lightweight and austere building. An ephemeral installation that emerges within an empty and hybrid container. The spatial organization consists of two volumes: one filled (sanitary facilities) and the other empty (the bar). Both are covered by a curved skin that forms the boundary between circulation and service areas. This skin not only serves as a boundary but also encloses usable spaces within the interstices formed by the filled volumes and the skin itself.

The lighting emerges as the protagonist, drawing silhouettes that shape the spatiality linearly, but also generating volumes depending on the space to be illuminated. Thus, the lighting defines the distinctive aspects of the proposal in its nocturnal version. The reinterpretation of elegance unfolds by incorporating rustic elements of the construction, which emerge transformed into luxurious objects: pendant lighting constructed from half metal tubes, galvanized fluted walls, backlit plastic ducts. Every detail reveals a play of contrasts, merging roughness and delicacy, reestablishing the guidelines for conceiving elegance with economical resources, but also an ephemeral elegance.

Through an industrial language of illumination, a regressive communication is woven, a temporal dialogue that suggests its ephemeral destiny. Time is present in its materials and also in its communication through a numerical countdown composed of light tubes controlled by a DMX system, just like the overall lighting.
Cien, an ephemeral ballet that transports us on a suspended journey through time, enveloping us in the magic of its forms and the poetry of its transitory existence.
clasico-quilmes: "Proud of what's ours" is not just the Quilmes beer company´s slogan, it explains between the lines a message whose identity must be seen in space. In this sense, we believe that Quilmes beer company image is not only that which could be related to traditional "bodegones y cantinas from Buenos Aires", it is above all its own history. They are its historical advertisements, its wooden beer creates, the history of its brewery, an example of the progress of an era.

The proposal of the project must be superior to what the image of what a typical " bares porteño" suggests, otherwise we will simply be replicating what many porteños bars have already developed. From the old and irreplaceable by authentic history, to the more than well-known reditions that already exist. That is why our proposal is strong in the use of elements that refer to the history of Quilmes beer and tell us about its true essence, without losing sight of the generic aesthetic framework of the still life in which it is contained.

We work with a composition that proposes emotion and sensitivity, that impacts from its scenographic bearing. Of viable production since the patinated galvanized pipes and the wooden boxes aged with bitumen are eventually massively replicable and do not require qualified labor.

A structure that unifies both from its synthesis and from its constructive and communicational coherence. An emotional selection of elements such as the factory with its characteristic silos, the traditional billboard of Mar del Plata city, the old beer boxes that adding the beertanks compose a space where the Quilmes universe merges.

All these elements are unified through multiple pipes of steel and galvanized sheet, illuminated in clear/dark. These instruments undoubtedly communicate by themselves the presence of a portion of factory accompanying the gastronomic experience.
The layout responds openly to the street, inviting all its passers-by to enter the premises, as if it were a kiosk, as our client suggested.
dos-casas-conde: From the outset this project had to answer two different voices — two clients. Both needed the same number of square metres for their future homes.

It is perhaps the greatest achievement of this project: working out how to fill the entire buildable volume equally for both owners, without either losing access to almost the full width and length of the plot. The strategy was to distribute the corresponding square metres crosswise, so that both units rotate centrifugally around the axis of the central courtyard.
To achieve the crossed connection between both properties without losing usable metres, we decided to take the stairs outside, like jet bridges linking the two units.
The building's silhouette results from filling the buildable volume to the maximum allowed by the Buenos Aires building code for that neighbourhood.

One strategy for making the most of the metres was to keep two areas of the former property, clearly shown through their exposed brick vaulted slabs, taking advantage of spaces that today's code for that neighbourhood would no longer permit. The new building also recalls the old spatial arrangement by sitting on the traces of the former courtyard house, adapting the old ground-floor layout to the two new homes.
Property A, ground floor plus two levels, has four rooms; property B, of the same height, has five. Both are stepped, freeing terraces at the front and at the rear.

The scheme treats the wall as an element separate from the structure. This shows on the front and rear elevations, driven by the intention of a solid masonry facade whose window openings work by subtraction, leaving the structure visible behind.

These voids were completed by a system of enclosures and balcony railings whose folds and textures set out to soften the light and to carry a continuous verticality across both facades, striking a balance of empty and solid bands against the large neutral wall volume of the whole.
The inner courtyard, which organises circulation centrifugally, has a traditional treatment of openings, giving the leading role in that space to its multidirectional stairs.

The greatest achievement of this project was fitting, within the traces of the old building, two homes whose volumetric ambition exceeded the capacity of the site — and, through a strategy of simple circulation links, managing to occupy the whole plot for both houses.
edificio-del-plata: Corresponds to offices: more than 600 office plots per square kilometre. Housing, meanwhile, accounts for 20%, with fewer than 200 residential plots per square kilometre…"

2020, pandemic, City of Buenos Aires. The city emptied of traffic and people. Its services closed, an internal migration towards the periphery. Microcentro suffered, as never before, the most serious abandonment since its beginnings as the city's financial district. As a result, the following years brought policies to reorganise land use through financing and new tax rules.

The population voids across the commercial and executive uses of the Microcentro blocks reveal a new demographic, which we used as the conceptual trigger for our proposal. This record of solids and voids is a device that lets us organise a compositional grid through a system of repeatable cells, applicable across several areas of intervention at different scales, materials and textures.

This cellular composition creates a map of textures that organises the flooring, the planting and the furniture, on both the roof terrace and the ground floor. It also works as a morphological piece that folds and allows a fractal play and, depending on how it is applied, gives shape to the various pieces that define the building's interior design. All of which, through its configuration, gives us a kind of texture map applicable to every area of intervention. Inside the studio flat the system appears again, materialised in a piece that works as a divider and a support for different uses, under the same formal premise.

In tectonic terms the material strategy sets out to partially dress the existing building while leaving the original visible. The project has an industrial character, with sand tones, greys, and certain highlights and glints focused in areas where a degree of sophistication stands out. The way the ceilings are applied lets the existing slab and its services show through the gaps, as part of a group of textures where the existing fabric and the contemporary intervention meet. The applied stone interventions speak to the existing concrete columns, whose rough bush-hammered treatment underlines that this is a container with a long history.

The ground floor is functionally integrated between the lobby and the shops through two large entrance portals, and visually integrated between the Pasaje Carabelas square and the Carlos Pellegrini pavement through a compositional system applied to the flooring and an artistic lighting ceiling running across the building. We added a reception space that resolves both entrances.
Given the building's multiple uses, the proposal addresses signage and environmental graphics as part of the holistic design of the scheme.

(grasses, salvias, lavenders and herbaceous plants) are organised within the cellular compositional system, as are its shallow-rooted trees (Aguaribay, Anacahuita, Bauhinia, Acer palmatum, citrus). The suspended artistic lighting object that acts as a ceiling also follows the same composition and fractal logic.

Besides conveying an industrial aesthetic, the chosen materials meet certain sustainability requirements: the suspended acoustic felt ceiling (made of 100% recyclable components), sprayed cellulose applied to the slab, the screen panel, and Geoclad SW 1520 sheet, among others.

We understand that an interior design proposal must meet not only compositional balance but conceptual coherence, where a criterion of "holistic design" allows the whole set of elements to be grasped as one.
elyaki: Two worlds, one door. In less than 60 square meters, a radical eclecticism unfolds: an entrance alley where the visual overload of neon, wet asphalt, projecting signs, and overhead cables takes center stage. Here, the atmosphere is unmistakably Yakitori—food on the go, urgency, the raw truth of the urban night. Yet behind the wall of weathered red brick lies another universe: Victoria Brown, a refined cocktail bar where Queen Victoria, transformed into a Geisha, presides over an atmosphere of sophistication.

The architecture becomes an act of revelation. The dividing wall is not merely a wall—it is a secret door, a shifting boundary. It slides, moves aside, and exposes what has been concealed. Facing the street: urgency, an aesthetic of chaos, a nocturnal palette of green and purple neon, industrial light poles, overlapping signs with ideograms, and weathered vinyl graphics. Raw materials prevail: brick, exposed wiring, and asphalt-textured paving.

Behind it: stillness. A cabinet of curiosities where Queen Victoria—dressed in a black and red kimono, with the sharp, dramatic gaze of Kabuki—reigns over bottles of distilled spirits. Warm, shifting light flickers across a fusion of Eastern and British ornamentation. Suspended industrial lighting coexists with intricately cut white paper lanterns.

The space operates as a paradox: one enters Yakitori as a tourist and discovers, as a traveler, a period cabinet of curiosities. The brick door is both metaphor and mechanism. Crossing its threshold means leaving behind the sensory rush of modern Tokyo and entering a suspended moment in time, where Victoria Geisha presides over each drink as an act of transformation. Neon and brocade coexist. Speed and ritual converge. Two Tokyos, one shared heartbeat.
fehgra: The project is based on the idea of creating a space that, given the characteristics of the client, seeks to create different situations related to the hotel and gastronomic experience.

It is a private gastronomic development center for FEHGRA (Federación Empresaria Hotelera y Gastronómica de la República Argentina). The complexity of resolving a great diversity of programmatic needs in just 1399sqf was addressed through the strategy of generating a route whose design and materiality decisions resolve the different situations of use, achieving a unique and integrating experience.

This route proposes to go through different stations that include a barism and cafeteria island, a cocktail bar island, a specialised library sector, a product exhibition area (tableware, accessories, etc.), a cellar room prepared for tastings and samplings, and finally an auditorium that ends in a show cooking island equipped with cutting-edge technology in terms of gastronomic equipment.

Each of these stations is designed as a sequence of granite blocks that, through their arrangement and size, recreate the passage from one island to another, generating an organic and monomaterial promenade. A vaulted ceiling inspired by the textures and materiality of the distillate barrels unifies the spaces, contributing to the sense of a journey. In the same way, the use of wooden planked cladding treated using the Shou Sugi Ban method appears throughout the entire project, delicately and elegantly reminiscent of wood burning in the fire and the kitchen. The general lighting was resolved with both spot and indirect lighting, but adding the design of pieces designed for the occasion and handcrafted to generate reflections and sparkles that allude to the dreamlike and festive sense of the world of sparkling wines.
fogon: The idea of a typical traditional London tavern, pub aesthetics was the premise of our client. In order to do so, we looked for concepts of the spirit of traditional British taverns, without falling into typical resources, nor losing the focus of the idea of a classic European restaurant with a contemporary artistic touch.

The proposal was based on the idea of resorting to materials that define this architectural aesthetic, although far from reproducing, we decided to extirpate only its DNA: "The windows of iron window frames and bare bricks. These two elements were then used in different ways throughout the venue and basically set the location’s mood.

The distribution scheme is divided into two levels. The kitchen area occupies 50% of the general floor on both levels, this is due to the great success of the food delivery business. That's why we've set up a delivery office in the back area.

The restaurant is divided into two different levels of use: The family area (first floor), and the men's area (ground floor), as indicated by the Muslim religion and is therefore the use of large boxes on the upper level.

On the facade of the Mall we have used a strategy to provide a differentiation from nearby shops, we raised a facade parallel to the existing one, through a system of metal beams and columns that support the same aesthetic language as the interior, same system of distributed glass structures and open-joint brick walls in a composition in conjunction with the double door access.

The compositional system of the bricks mutes to become "aerial" walls, with open joints crossed by screwed rods. This gave us an ethereal composition that allows us to resolve the proposal in a non-linear way to the original suggestion of a traditional London tavern.
We have taken into consideration the weight of these walls and it was essential to use structural calculations and fasteners specifically located in various areas of the existing walls.

The idea was to interlace through an interior skin system that covered all the walls and the most outstanding functional spaces. This great system is composed by an organization of bricks and windows. We developed a metal framework system, a kind of breezy brick lattice that is vaguely reminiscent of the mashrabiya, a kind of projecting oriel window characteristic of Arabic residences, in this case much less ornate than the traditional carved woodwork.

Glazed sections have different levels of transparency, in some cases without glasses and in others with old glasses or translucent or opaque glasses organized according to the functionality of each space, referencing the smoked glass of British pubs. This system of glass structure accompanies the entire interior, not only as a decorative system, but also performs as division between public areas and services areas, such as bathroom, kitchen.
The wooden cladding on the bar and floor are references to the pub and also add a touch of warmth to the environment, underscored by the partially coffered ceiling featuring floral decorations.

The most important challenge as designers and creators of spaces, is undoubtedly that it achieves a unique and singular characteristic through elements recognizable by the consumer. That's why Fogon alludes to the usual material language of English pubs but we have interpreted it in such a way that it fits in with an overcoming and authentic idea.
fresco: From the beginning we understood that the brand is, as its name indicates ( Fresco means Fresh in spanish ), a place whose identity is marked by the nature it self, that reminds the freshness and naturally products of this venue. From this reflection we have suggested to implement a nature of alive presence with a clear design implementation of it.

The project has been influenced by modern, neutral and industrial details. The neutrality is given by the balance of its materials and its shades of white. All its materials have been used in a bitonal balance of black and white, except for details in corrugated aluminium and the black rubber floor.

The façade is a direct reference to the modern architectural style as a result of a modular organization. The use of metal meshes of different depths and the incorporation of huge cylinders of vegetation recreate a scene in which modern architecture meets nature.

The use of mesh allows us to visualize the old façade, suggesting an effort to preserve the heritage of the original building while applying a contemporary touch. With this operation we have managed to unify the outline of the facade.
This nature is form and function in all its interventions, they work as a light system and as an active landscape in several of its bars.

Same strategy drove us to use metallic mesh system in all the perimeter bar facing the hall. Above this double height atrium, six large lighting fixtures hang from the ceiling surrounded by vegetation. The species of vegetation used are ferns, various philodendrons, various ferns, Potus lemon or green, Calatheas, Dracenas, Zamioculcas, Crotones, Spatyfilium and so on. We propose an eco- perceived experience, in which most visitors feel as if they were in an old greenhouse or garden with elements that simulate magical vegetation

We have extended the upper floor by building and connecting, as a bridge, between two previously unconnected areas on the first floor. This unified the entire upper floor crowned by a large perimeter bar.
galeria-objeto-a: The building is located on Niceto Vega Street, an artery in constant development in the Palermo neighbourhood. From the outset, the project recognised the importance of the building's presence through both its architectural expression and its programme.

The speed and lights that characterise the street became a starting point for reflecting on the duality between the building's outward expression and its inner world. The facade therefore acts as an inflection point between a static, perceptive interior and a dynamic exterior closely linked to passing traffic.

The project preserves the most genuine characteristics of the original Palermo house and integrates the new intervention through a contemporary language that also pays tribute to the existing construction.

The relationship between facade and street was reinterpreted as a backlit sign: a playful, moving field of colour. This agile and lightweight operation rests on the robustness of the original facade, composing a closely related tectonic whole.

A sequence of twelve slender pivoting shutters, made of frosted polycarbonate in metal frames, allows the facade to shift from completely closed to fully open. Each shutter conceals an RGB LED system that can colour the facade according to the desired chromatic sequence.

Inside, the building is organised in section through stepped courtyards, floating mezzanines and quiet spaces for perception and contemplation. Continuous views connect the rooms with the exterior, natural light, the sky and the vegetation, while metal frames hold large panes of glass independently from the reinforced concrete structure.

The project captures a planted oasis and makes it an integral part of the building, preserving the essence and character of the original house. Throughout the work, particular attention was paid to the points where the old house and the new gallery meet, from the main architectural decisions down to the smallest construction details.

Technologically, the project follows the same principle: an early twentieth-century house incorporates contemporary systems, from energy-conscious air conditioning to high-definition audio and video. The spatial richness, noble materials, constructive honesty, chromatic calm and preserved greenery create a setting that gives full prominence to the works of art it contains.
goodsten: GOODSTEN isn´t just a creamery. It is born from an experience of oneiric landscapes, as if it where form another world, with a completely different logic. Unknown and fantastic lands made us think of precious stones. Their faceted surfaces inspired us to create a construction system. Those rocks, which blind us with their glows and crystal-like textures, are diamonds from another world.

The allegory of the precious stone had an impact on creative decisions, both in design and construction aspects, branding decisions, and even on the making of the desserts, which are prepared on granite slabs with temperatures below zero.

We transformed this idea into a construction system, through a material which allowed us to mold these faceted figures, without falling into the literalness of stony materials. We wanted to express a homogeneity through one continuous surface of elements which set up a diamond-like shell, made possible by means of the repetition of treated metallic tiles.

The proposal is expressive and synthetic, in a way that it suggests an intriguing formalism from its silent and mono material condition. The construction of a double height annex, which grants the true spatiality to the creamery, is attached to the original house so that both coexist in a respectful and harmonic way. The new diamond-like structure dialogues morphologically with the pitched roofs of a 20th century chalet.

The site of the annex incorporates two mansards in the inside and a third one on the outside, which respond to the requirements of the ventilating and lighting municipal codes. Because of this, the roof considerably modifies its shape allowing the needed lighting and fresh air to enter. As a result, we found ourselves with a very plastic roof, geometrically speaking. At ground level we built a concrete piece, which works as a basement over which the roof rests, becoming one similar morphological configuration.

We created a compositional system of triangles and faceted surfaces which can be seen in various elements particularly designed. From the openings in the building in the production zone, to the annex roof allowing the light to be sifted. The same geometry, also makes up the metallic structure of the general lighting system, as well as the design of the exterior floorings, made from precast concrete. It all comes together to the same compositional criteria.

The general interior idea is determined by essentials from the aesthetic Nordic imaginary, as are the skin and leather tapestry, walls coated in natural wood and light-colored granites. All of these noble materials are used in a monochromatic way, so that a perfect integration of the oneiric and fantastic world and the compositional system created is generated with no greater difficulty.

The client´s requirements have been very rigorous. The surface destined to the production area covers almost 50% of the buildings total surface, divided in two levels and with two double circulations as to ensure the clearly differentiated public and private areas.
hausscape: This is a façade intervention in the Design District area of Miami, characterized by its elaborate and brilliantly designed catalog of facades. Although the intervention on the existing building measuring 132 feet x 60 feet (40 meters x 18 meters) had to consider this influential environment, it was conceived as understated rather than provocative, in line with the brand's commercial proposal.

The façade intervention was carried out on a 40-year-old building made of concrete and masonry, with its entire shell preserved. The existing building is 14 feet tall and features five large windows and two entrances crowned with their canopies.

The strategy involved subtly concealing the various functional elements of the façade using a skin whose silhouette allows the original building to remain visible. This taller skin was designed with custom folds and perforations, preserving the openings of the original building.

The proposal addresses the strong winds typical of South Florida through various perforations. The attachment system is mechanical, using screws at all connections, including its attachment to the existing building.

The structure consists of steel with an aluminum framework, and it incorporates 42 different types of custom-folded aluminum panels, 3 mm thick and painted in a warm white color (milky white). These 42 panels are all the same height, totaling 238 folded panels interconnected in a continuous series of folds. Each panel was specifically designed to be precisely attached to the functional requirements of the existing building, which remained unaltered.

Designed with a continuous series of folds at different rhythms, the façade gains movement and dynamics, reinforcing the longitudinality of the building. Three specific areas are accentuated with deeper folds, suggesting a different function on the façade. The customized design of the folds allows for a play of depths where lighting maximizes its visual impact.

The system was designed to function as a whole, meaning the panels are interconnected to cover the mechanical anchoring points of the system. All paneling is mounted on aluminum tubes, which are not visible behind the system, suggesting a modular presence. The various folds serve as an economical and sustainable design resource, resulting in a subtle and understated order for the façade.

As previously explained, the Miami Design District was essentially conceived as a highly spectacular catalog of facades, which made us consider the strategy we should employ to achieve a dialogue with the rest of the facades, while facing the challenge of a very low-cost budget compared to the others. We decided to create a modular system using affordable materials, with an emphasis on personalized and sustainable design. As a result, we designed tall modules [4'-1 1/2"] that can be transported in a container, easily transported to the site, and ultimately, easy to handle for installation. This economical and sustainable design approach resulted in an orderly and understated aesthetic proposal.

We emphasize the work carried out by the professional office, valuing the attributes specifically tailored to the project. The development of each piece was carefully planned to minimize material waste. The dimensions were studied to simplify maritime transport. Lastly, each piece was designed for assembly, ensuring easy manipulation and construction.
hyatt-ziva: BEACH RESTAURANT

Our analysis is based on an organizational and representative guiding idea. Organizational because it defines the layout where the hierarchies and locations of the sitting system are resolved. Representative because we understand that the material must be a tectonic and poetic condition to generate the determining DNA of the project. The sugar canes whose production is of marked influence in Central America is the poetic language whose technical resolution we propose in bamboo canes, which offers a lot of constructive versatility. Its particularity allows us to understand it as a design element. The formal resolution, we propose it through a construction of waves that emulate the waters of the ocean. The indivisible link between the logical definition of a beach restaurant and the collective imaginary of waves. The cladding, flooring, furniture and decoration are resolved with materials and colors that refer to nature, the sea and its connection with both elements. Other decisions, such as the use of ropes and nets that give character to architectural and decorative elements, are part of this world that connects this sector with its immediate surroundings.
LOBBY

The conceptual design is rooted in an aesthetic inspired by the typical pitched roofs of Caribbean homes, preserving all their components, from beams and trusses to wooden shingles and rafters, right down to the tiles and skylights. Two spaces housing a bar and reception were crafted while maintain the weathered roof tile materials and greenery, as if they were part of an authentic Caribbean home where the passage of time has seamlessly integrated nature with architecture. Shutters are employed to functionally divide both side entrances, further emphasizing the symbolic language woven throughout the entire space. Furniture selection has been carefully curated to harmonize the hotel with its natural environment. The presence of fixtures inspired by local fauna and the marine ambiance, featured in both lighting and decor, heightens the feeling of connectivity with the surrounding nature.
CORRIDORS

These spaces function as pathways connecting the 5 buildings. Our design approach has centered around neutral and understated materials, focusing on subtle changes in texture rather than color shifts. We have preserved the presence of natural, matte wood tones, along with textured light grays. Hints of green emerge through carefully curated vegetation, which included preserved moss wall and native plants. A striking suspended structure, reminiscent of the commercial boats found in Barbado´s port, stretches across the entire length of these circular areas. The artisanal and vernacular design of the furniture maintains the overall style while emphasizing a deep reverence for tradition.
PREFERRED RECEPTION

This prominent and sophisticated space within the complex should be showcased as a preferential and hierarchical area. Therefore, we find in vernacular art and culture a communication channel to represent the unique and detailed aesthetics of this complex area. It is a space that invites us to immerse ourselves in the tradition of Barbados, from its role as a commercial port in the Americas, while also acknowledging its pre-Columbian origins. A suspended structure that emulates ancient commercial boats, along with the presence of stacked rocks as a nod to pre-Columbian origins. A suspended structure that emulates ancient commercial boats, along with the presence of stacked rocks as a nod to pre-Columbian culture, both serve as major focal points.  Details such as an interior oasis of native vegetation, combined with organic furniture and materials like cane, contribute to the integration of vernacular aesthetics.
LOBBY BAR

Its design language forms an integral part of the central lobby, mirroring the approach taken in the coffee lounge area. Its functional structure seamlessly blends with the overall space, with a distinct orientation towards the pool and the beach. Roof tiles, coral stone, and lush vegetation are the dominant elements that contribute to crafting this environment where nature harmoniously coexists with the bar area, serving as an organizing element. This space, characterized by the size of the roof tiles, both modulates and provides purpose to the bottle area. The furniture, once again, evokes a strong connection with the natural surroundings.
COFFEE LOUNGE

This area constitutes an annex to the coffee space, yet it is seamlessly integrated with the hotel´s common areas. Given this, the aesthetics should harmoniously blend with the hotel´s shared spaces. As a strategic choice, we have incorporated a hanging representation of reinterpretations of boats in the circulation area, mirroring what we´ve done in the preferred reception. The central area of the coffee lounge is covered by a substantial wooden pergola and shaded by parasols that resemble shutters. This space´s functionality is intertwined with the coffee shop and prioritizes the views, so the seating layout must be highly adaptable and, above all, playful. Materials such as weathered rooftiles create visually striking corners that are perfect for social media snapshots. Finally, the greenery and paving materials simulate stones and cobblestones, enhancing the overall ambiance.
COFFEE SHOP

The café pays tribute to the historical tradition of the cobblestone streets of the colonial city through its most evocative symbol: the shutters of Caribbean homes. Ceramic brick, another characteristic element, serves as cladding in front of the counter and suggest a more contemporary language. In contrast to the traditional style of shutters, a prominent elliptical element, simple and modern in design, stands out as a central piece in both lighting and decoration. This fusion of the classic and the contemporary reflects the duality between the past and the future that defines this place. The colors chosen in its materials, such as browns, ochres, and natural tones, blend harmoniously with the coffee color, creating integration though tones and textures.
BUFFET

The space features the iconic presence of sugar cane as a prominent and standout element. It is used both in its simple form and intricately worked and cut to create alternative and functional uses. Sugar cane, whose production significantly influences Central America, serves as the poetical language for all the key elements within this space. We propose its technical resolution using bamboo canes, which offer considerable construction versatility. The inclusion of native vegetation and green walls inside, along with the use of coral cladding, come together to create a space that embodies as a strong connection to nature.
ASIAN RESTAURANT

We have drawn inspiration from certain Asian philosophical concepts, such as the beauty of imperfection, the appreciation of the incomplete, and subtle refinement that doesn´t flaunt itself, speak, or show off, but rather hints at it. These concepts have been translated into our space. The upper cladding, which modulates voids and solids, emphasizes “the incomplete” and is constructed using wood treated with the “Yakisugi” method. The soft pink tones directly relate to the subtle refinement that doesn´t boast. The large lamps have been reimagined as furniture pieces. We have incorporated recognizable elements and symbols from everyday Asian culture, such as Oriental lanterns reimagined as prominent furniture pieces, kakemonos, and Noreen curtains, all contributing to the presence of Asian culture in our restaurant. We have focused on three significant objects that emulate Oriental lanterns and serve as the focal points: the show cooking areas. Lastly, an element at the entrance mimics an artistically composed archeological piece.
BEACH RESTAURANT

The beach restaurant offers a nuanced perspective of the Caribbean coastal region’s natural beauty. The cladding, flooring, furniture, and decor incorporate materials and colors that evoke the essence of nature and the sea, establishing a profound connection with both elements. Additional design choices, such as the incorporation of nautical ropes and fishing nets, infuse character into architectural and decorative components, seamlessly integrating into the environment that surrounds this space. Our formal design solutions centers around the creation of wave-like structures that emulate the ocean´s rhythmic patterns. These waves are crafted from bamboo wood, chosen for its construction versatility and its cultural significance in this region.
ITALIAN RESTAURANT

Italy has wielded two significant influences throughout ancient and recent history: first, through the existence of the Roman Empire, and more recently, though its cultural and culinary impact following World War II. Arches and domes held paramount importance in the ancient world until the Renaissance period. Both elements take center stage in this space. The domes, in the midst of their construction process and surrounded by scaffolding, conjure the notion of a possible atelier reminiscent of Leonardo Da Vinci´s. The entire ambiance of the space ins imbued with a materiality that draws inspiration from the aesthetic of romantic Italy: brick, limestone ceramics, wooden structures and textiles. The architectural presence of Italian neorealism, paired with mecano-style shelving and furnishings, offers a contemporary language that reflects a more present-day Italy.
SPORT BAR

Barbados is rich in culture, history, gastronomy and sports. The sports bar is inspired by its iconic drink, rum, and the national sport: cricket. These two elements combined inspire us to create z gathering place that invites people to explore the island´s history and generates a sense of enjoyment and fun. The old barrels and stills of its distilleries, where this national drink is prepared, inspire the colors, textures, and patterns of the space´s cladding. The presence of historical, informative, and advertising images of rum helps those who visit understand the importance of this beverage for the island.
POOL BAR

The essence of the beach, encapsulated in the sand, the language of corals, and the maritime breeze, has been our guiding inspiration for this space. Given its elevated location within the building, we have embraced the winds as an integral part of the experience by incorporating long fabrics hanging from the ceiling. Sandy tones define the aesthetics of the furniture and its textures, while the coral motif is elegantly brought to life through perforated metal sheets that take center stage by adorning the bar´s backdrop. In certain design elements, we have infused an aesthetic reminiscent of the glamour and style of vintage-era swimmers. This purposeful design choice accentuates the presence of the adjacent pool, enhanced by a bar that offers a direct view, creating a seamless connection between the two spaces.
iguanafix: The Iguanafix offices are conceived through a direct and essential architectural approach, where materiality expresses the company’s identity and operational character.

The project incorporates natural OSB panels and exposed tubular steel structures, elements closely associated with the construction industry that become an integral part of the architectural language. Materials are presented without cladding or unnecessary finishes, highlighting their texture, construction logic, and functional nature.

Glass and OSB partitions organize the different work areas, promoting transparency, visual integration, and interaction between teams. Modular shelving systems also serve as furniture, storage, and spatial dividers.

Natural light is complemented by a targeted LED spotlight system, emphasizing materials and surfaces. Graphic communication is integrated into the architecture through vinyl graphics applied directly to the glass partitions.

The overall design is conceived as a flexible, modular, and adaptable system, capable of evolving alongside the company’s changes and growth. It is an architecture in constant transformation, where materials, structure, and furniture come together to create an identity that is consistent with the spirit of Iguanafix.
indusparquet: The project developed for Indus Parquet, a Brazilian company specialising in the production and installation of timber flooring with more than 80 years of experience, emerged as an architectural interpretation of the values of sustainability, traceability and connection with nature that define the brand. Located in the Nunez neighbourhood, the flagship store offers an immersive experience in which wood is presented in its purest and most essential state. The project draws inspiration from the controlled planting and harvesting processes the company carries out in different regions of Brazil, incorporating a spatial narrative connected to the forest landscape and the organic origin of the raw material.

The architectural proposal is structured around an orthogonal composition of exposed natural logs, used as facade elements, cladding and to shape the topography of the outdoor entrance. This approach plane acts as a sculptural surface that organises the relationship with the public realm and creates both a physical and perceptual threshold from the pavement. Inside, the space unfolds through a winding, non-linear route inspired by the experience of moving through a forest, connecting areas for display, customer service and material exploration.

At the centre of the project is a series of floor-to-ceiling pivoting structures displaying more than forty varieties of wood and finishes. A creative table provides a place for architects, clients and brand advisers to work together. The route culminates on an upper level intended for meetings, events and gastronomic experiences, integrating a landscaped terrace, designer furniture, signature pieces, specialised lighting and artworks. Together, these elements consolidate a complete brand experience in which architecture, landscape, art and materiality operate as a single narrative system.
iol: Designing workplaces for the fintech world involves the challenge of translating a complex digital ecosystem into architecture: speed and technological innovation coexisting with solidity and institutional backing. In the case of IOL (Invertir Online), one of the sector's unicorn companies and a key part of Grupo Supervielle, the project called for a tectonic identity that would reflect its leadership and dynamism. With this conceptual premise, we developed its new offices on the 23rd floor of the QIUB building in Palermo.

Working on the 23rd floor, with an open plan exposed to panoramic views, our first design decision was not to fragment the urban landscape. We designed a functional capsule: a compact central core that concentrates and contains all the company's fixed, technical and service functions, including coffee point, pantry, toilets, copy point, storage areas, booths and data centre. This geometric operation acts as the heart of the floor, freeing the building's perimeter. As a result, every occupied workstation faces the glazed facade, ensuring full natural light and democratising views of the city for the entire team.

The perimeter around this central capsule is organised as a fluid space, avoiding the monotony of a conventional large open-plan office. The programme is divided according to specific patterns of use that respond to contemporary working methods: operational areas designed for maximum acoustic and lighting comfort, helping staff to focus while giving every position an outward view; collaborative areas that encourage spontaneous exchange, group synergy and meetings of different kinds, whether formal or relaxed; and a breakout zone strategically placed at the end of the floor's radial circulation, conceived as an informal setting supported by the capsule's fixed functions.

The material proposal seeks a restrained and warm expression that conveys IOL's solidity as a company. Bespoke furniture and lighting design play leading roles in shaping the atmosphere of the office. The contrast between the tectonic opacity of the central service block and the transparent permeability of the operational areas creates a continuous visual balance. The result is a space that not only meets the client's demanding technical and operational requirements, but also establishes itself as an efficient, flexible and transparent work of corporate architecture.
juan-valdez: In every space of Buenos Aires´s Juan Valdez, the essence of Colombian coffee is reflected, connecting the product’s origin with a new local identity. The colonial tiles that line the walls evoke coffee farms, while the lighting fixtures resemble traditional roofs, creating a warm and inviting atmosphere.

The petiribí wood used in the furniture adds solidity and naturalness, complemented by jute, which introduces a warm texture typical of Latin America. A piece of furniture specifically designed to showcase the products becomes a distinctive feature, aligned with the brand’s visual identity.

Artistic wooden details and pastel tones on the walls represent the Colombian coffee landscapes, bringing a touch of color that connects visitors to the nature of the product. The result is a space where coffee is the protagonist, surrounded by materials that reinforce its authenticity and Latin American origin.
kavak-hub: Kavak is a company dedicated to the sale of used vehicles, leader in the Mexican market. The first step of this unicorn company to regionalize its business was Argentina. For this reason the identity came from the mother company, but it only had the graphic identity development.

Our job was to receive the directives on the guidelines on the functional organization used in Mexico, add the palette of materials, and with all this compose a sober tonal balance that accurately represents the brand. Therefore, we had to develop a tectonic identity linked to the graphic identity generated in Kavak Mexico. This is how we investigated materials that define the brand as is the example of the black corrugated sheet metal, the proposed furniture, lighting, which have been a key part of this new identity.

We explored and developed the resource of diagonals as an expression associated with the letter K, which can be verified from the windows, the lighting layout, and the metallic divisions & vegetation that shape the delimitation of the open space whose areas are divided by the consultation of the sample case and reception.

The space comprises a 300-square-meter customer service showroom (with a reception area, a meeting room and 14 terminals for consulting the sample collection), a comprehensive vehicle inspection center for on-the-spot vehicle condition assessment, and a further 15,000 square meters with the capacity to house up to 700 cars from the company's inventory.
kavak-oficinas: Kavak is a used-car company founded in Mexico and a leader in the Latin American market. Argentina was this unicorn's first step in taking the brand regional. Its identity therefore came from the parent company, but consisted mainly of graphic and branding work.

Our project starts from the programmatic reading and functional organisation used in Mexico, proposes the palette of materials, and with all of it composes a balance that carries the brand's values into architecture. That meant developing a tectonic identity tied to the graphic identity created at Kavak Mexico.

So we researched materials that define the brand, proposing finishes such as straight corrugated sheet, brick tiles, exposed concrete, and fabrics and folders designed by our team. The furniture and lighting are also leading elements of this new identity.

We explored and developed diagonals as an expression tied to the brand book, using them to resolve the facade, the layout of the lighting, and the metal dividers and planting that delimit the open space and organise it.

The offices sit in the former Philips factory in Argentina and have a distinctive industrial character, which paired perfectly with the tectonic aesthetic we developed in the materials for Kavak. The space covers 800 m², laid out mainly through the repetition of boxes at its centre that divide the open-plan areas strategically to avoid the "one big space" effect. These characteristic boxes are clad in white sheet on the outside and work as islands, housing phone booths, informal meeting rooms, lockers and seating.

The space is broadly divided into two open-plan areas, for tech and for dining. At the far end of the offices are the call centre and two large meeting rooms. A tiered seating area with furniture was designed specifically for informal use.
luccianos-caballito: From the outset, the brand sought to move away from the preconceptions of a traditional ice cream shop and align itself with aesthetic qualities that are unconventional for this type of programme. As designers, we chose to bring the product and the brand closer to art from several perspectives. Through the selection of materials, lighting, furniture and certain almost sculptural devices, we gave the ice cream shop qualities that evoke the comfort of a domestic living room and the atmosphere of an art gallery.

Through the development of different construction elements - the bush-hammered treatment of the columns, exaggerating the qualities of the concrete; the vertical rhythm of the black timber slats; and, above all, the work on the iron and glass cladding and balustrade - the design consistently seeks to enhance the spatial qualities of the premises, focusing on its double-height volume.

The balance between old and contemporary, monochrome and colourful, smooth and textured elements creates an engaging aesthetic eclecticism that always gives centre stage to the product being sold: ice cream.
luccianos-olivos: The initial pursuit of the brand was to draw away from the preconception of the traditional ice cream shop and relate to somewhat unconventional aesthetics for this type of stores. Therefore, to bring the product and brand together with different forms of art was the path chosen as designers. Through the election of materials, lighting, equipment and some semi-sculptural elements, we were able to incorporate into the ice cream shop attributes that convey the comfort of domestic living and reminiscences of an art gallery or jewelry store.

Through the development of different constructive elements - the hammered treatment of the columns that exacerbates the characteristics of concrete; the verticality of the black wood siding; the elaborate piece of iron and glass that serves both as centerpiece and railing of the upper level- the goal is to enhance the spatial qualities of the store an put the focus of attention on its double height.

The construction of a topographic art piece was in part a decision associated with the idea of ​​gastronomic product with relevance in the artistic concept. Its location was decisive for its protagonism.

The balance of old / contemporary, monochromatic / colorful, flat / textured, generates an interesting aesthetic eclecticism that at all times gives way to promote the product in question: frozen creams.
malabia: Given its location in Palermo, a few metres from Plaza Armenia and in the middle of a residential and commercial area, the M1918 project sets out to answer the high demand for studio flats — for residential or professional use — with units of real spatial quality.

The building occupies the whole plot, creating a compact, homogeneous buildable volume which, divided into three blocks carved out by internal courtyards, houses all 22 units. Three residential levels plus two basement parking levels complete the 2,405 m² built.
The building's silhouette comes from making the most of the buildable volume the Buenos Aires building code allows for this site. A single core resolves vertical circulation throughout.

The entrance offers an arrival experience in the manner of a crossing a semi-urban pavement, double height, and passing through the intermittent covered stretches set by the blocks above. Green walls, courtyards and side planters, together with the double-height covered areas, turn the entrance into a genuine journey.

Starting from the client's requirement for the maximum number of units, each of small area, the design set out from the first to bring spatial quality to every one of them, flooding them with natural light and giving them generous, private outdoor space. The strategy was to resolve each block with two units per floor, set crosswise to the party walls, so as to free the longest facade in every case and place the openings there. Every unit has its own outdoor space: private, generous, green and bright. This explains the decision to set the building back from the street line, creating a buffer between the street facade and the building's own facade, with balcony terraces in that space.
In the “encastre” between courtyards and interior spaces lies the fullest expression of the project.

The use of material seeks a visual chromatic homogeneity. Both the street facade and the interior ones are resolved by showing the complexity of the structure — exposed concrete — accompanied by the openings, large panes of glass that adjust to the rules the concrete sets in each case.

We have proposed conceptual elements in your showcase, in addition to two other corners, represented by broken and discarded crockery that offer an artistic image that adds to theimagination of your guests.
